Volumetric 3-component velocimetry measurements were taken of the flow field near a Rushton turbine in a stirred tank reactor.
The flow field was characterized by a strong radial jet, large tank-scale ring vortices, and small-scale blade tip vortices.
Approximately 15,000 3D velocity vectors were obtained in a cubic measurement volume.
Measurements were performed at three Reynolds numbers: 15,000, 107,000, and 137,000.

Three methods were used to identify the blade tip vortices: calculation of circumferential vorticity, calculation of local pressure minima via an eigenvalue approach ('λ2'), and calculation of swirling strength via an eigenvalue approach ('λci').
The 'swirl strength' criterion provided the clearest identification of the tip vortices.
Visualization of tip vortices up to 140 degrees past blade passage was observed in the highest Reynolds number case (137,000), which had not been previously shown.
The associated video can be viewed in MPEG-2 and MPEG-1 formats.
The related article was published in the online first section of Experiments in Fluids (2009), doi 10.1007/s00348-009-0711-9.
A Rushton turbine is a type of impeller used in stirred tank reactors, which are commonly used in chemical and biochemical processes.
Comprehensive characterization of the flow field around a Rushton turbine is important for optimizing the design and operation of stirred tank reactors.
The study provides the most comprehensive view to date of the flow field around a Rushton turbine, especially at the three different Reynolds numbers.
The volumetric nature of the data enabled tip vortex identification, vortex trajectory analysis, and calculation of vortex strength.
The highly unsteady, three-dimensional flow field around the Rushton turbine is a challenging flow to characterize experimentally.
Volumetric 3-component velocimetry is a powerful technique for measuring complex, 3D flow fields in detail.
